Monty Roberts - The Horse Whisperer

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Horse Whisperer Monty Roberts, lets us in on the secret language of Horses

Summary:
Monty Roberts is the ‘horse whisperer’ ….His autobiography The Man who Listens to Horses remained on the New York bestsellers list for 58 weeks. It was a word of mouth sensation selling nearly 6 million copies unheard of for a horse book. He has the Queen of England’s ear, having regularly advised her on her horses.
Now he will be in South Africa, to demonstrate and teach us how to communicate with horses.
Roberts believes that horses use a non-verbal language, which he terms "Equus," and that humans can use this language to communicate with horses.
The moment a human has earned the horse’s trust is called Join-Up®. Equus is a silent language of gestures like signing for the deaf. It’s the Rosetta Stone for the student of horses, and to see Monty crack the code on the language of Equus with horses who have had a past or wild tendencies it’s extraordinary.
Monty says he “didn’t create a set of methods, but only discovered what nature put in place long before humans domesticated horses 6000 years ago”. His father was horse trainer and a violent man, as a child, Monty worked with the horses, rejecting his father’s traditional and violent ways.
In Monty’s word’s “Violence is never the answer. Violence is always for the violator and never for the victim. No one of us was born with the right to say 'You must, or I’ll hurt you’ to any other being, animal or human.”
We will not only see Monty at work, calming and communicating undisciplined horses
“During the shows he communicates with horses he has never met and horses that have problems either loading into a box of letting people near them . People were asked to submit details of horses and Monty’s crew selected a few. Its an entertaining show.
..but also go with him to visit the Shumbashaba kids near Diepsloot…these are children from the surrounding areas who are being taught horse skills, these kids are not only riders but also have won medals vaulting .

Press Release:


Horse Whisperer
Can subtle behavioural language used by horses to communicate with each other be used by humans too? Carte Blanche catches up with Monty Roberts, the so-called Horse Whisperer, to witness his unusual techniques used to interact with horses - from those belonging to the world’s rich and famous, to those that children at the Shumbashaba horse programme ride in Diepsloot.


Script:


Link
Monty Roberts is famous around the world for his remarkable ability to persuade an unbroken horse to accept a saddle and rider in less than 30 minutes a process that normally takes several weeks

V/O
And 20 minutes later

Monty: It takes 4 to 6 weeks to break a horse traditionally its 30 minutes to have him accept first saddle and first rider if you take violence away and you use the communication system of the horse..

V/O 9 sec
At 81 Monty spends around 300 days of the year on the road. I’s his life’s work to bring horses and humans into a partnership

Monty: Well you have to do these things when you’re young. When I get old I am going to have to slow down.

V/O
Monty was born with horse fever running through his veins. He was in the saddle at age two; his father had a riding school in California.

Monty: So if he produced a son that won everything, then they would send their children to his school.
Derek: So you were part of his marketing?
Monty: I was his calling card so I showed his first horse when I was four and it went on from here until I won 11 world championships; but I never had a childhood. It was a unique upbringing that had a lot of problems with it,

V/O 5 sec
The main problem,for Monty, was his father’s treatment of the horses in his stable..

Monty: He was an extremely violent man, even for his times, and not only with his own horses but with me too. He would beat me to submission once a week just to be sure I was on the path….

Link
Monty was sent out to round up some wild horses for a rodeo show at the tender age of 13, and while he was observing those mustangs in Nevada, he picked up some aspects of their behaviour which were about to change his life

Derek: You are observing the mustangs - what went on in your mind?
Monty: That there was a better way... it's so emotional for me…Every time a person asks me a question like that I think of what my father did and how innocent those horses are and they are just horses; they are just wild, they are flight animals they mean no harm to anybody. I saw them relating to one another and I watched the lions stalking them - mountain lions, our puma, and I got to know the fight animal and the flight animal that way. And it's what turned my mind to say I want to study behavioural sciences -where you try to figure why we do what we do.
Derek: You noticed almost a code in their behaviour. What was that?
Monty: I started to notice the ear and the tongue and the neck and the head and the direction they travelled and the speed they travel all mean something and I went home wit 150 mustangs in trucks. I went in with those wild horses in fairly large enclosures with 50 horses in an enclosure and there was one day and one horse in a situation …that responded to me with my body movements, I tried to emulate some of his moves and he responded to them and he came to me, not because I responded as a predator, but because I responded as a flight animal, dropping my eyes moving to a 45 degree. That was a critical thing.

V/O 13 sec
And from that age on Monty, rejecting his father’s violent training methods, began to explore this revolutionary technique of natural horsemanship.

Derek: Totally impromptu passing by... and you noticed the horse wanted to play?
Monty: The horse is a little bored out here and a new guy comes by and he's saying hello, playing a game and having some fun. If I just go at him strong and square on eye on eye going to take charge of his safety and go away from me and then when I drop off he will stop and check me out….but…so I will keep coming…and when he looks back at me I will give him that move and just draw him off on a 45 degree angle to say, ah you’re okay... I guess you’re not going to kill me.

Derek: Term you use when you’ve cracked the code and started to bond with the horse in a special way?
Monty: Join Up…Ya that moment when a horse decides to be with you rather than away from you.

Link
Monty’s autobiography the man who listens to horses remained on the NYT bestseller lists for 58 weeks and sold more than six million copies. Nobody was more surprised than Monty Roberts.

Monty: To say I was surprised is the understatement of the century because I was taken to a publisher who said, 'look we will print it, but it won't pay for the printing. It will sell 3 000, max 5 000 copies'.

V/O 5 sec
In Johannesburg Monty visited Shumbashaba, a community horse school near Diepsloot.

Up sound

V/O
Monty started helping people, using horses back in 1955. It’s a cause he is passionate about and here at Shumabashaba he was moved by the potential of some of these children and their trainer…

Monty: You can see the love in their heart and it’s a very important thing you’re doing.

V/O
Perhaps this is Monty’s special gift- that he walks with crowds and Kings... or in this case the Queen...

Derek: Must be many stories; would working with the Queens horses be one of them?
Monty: Of course it would, sure.
Derek: Did you meet her
Monty : Many times…and I believe her to be the most influential world leader on the face of the earth and the most influential person for good that I have ever known

V/O 14 sec
When Monty Roberts began his journey, his ideas on how to train horses were hugely controversial, but he’s stayed the course and remains steadfast in his goal to leave the world a better place for horses…and humans

Monty: I persisted and carried on because I don’t think I had a choice.
Horses were my whole life; they were everything to me. If I had a chance to get the world to change and see the fallacy of violence, how could I fail to take that chance?
